On November 3, 2026, Spokane County SWAT deputies were dispatched to a rural property near Spangle, Washington, after an injured woman reached a neighbor’s home seeking emergency aid. Law enforcement quickly confirmed an active domestic crisis where an armed suspect had taken the lives of his mother and sister before barricading himself inside the residence.

Knowing that innocent lives hung in the balance, SWAT team members moved in to rescue potential survivors and secure the home. As Deputy Parker Perry, a dedicated K9 handler with his partner Brego, and Deputy Mason Acheson, an experienced SWAT sniper and former Washington State Trooper, advanced toward the entrance, the barricaded suspect opened fire without warning.

Both deputies were critically injured in the ambush while shielding their fellow officers. Team members immediately returned fire, safely pulled their wounded brothers from the line of fire, and contained the scene. Deputy Acheson, 35, passed away the following morning. Deputy Perry, 29, remained on life support until his family made the selfless choice to donate his organs, continuing to save lives even after his final watch.

Both men were Washington Army National Guard veterans, devoted husbands, and loving fathers who left behind young children, with Deputy Perry’s wife currently expecting their third baby. Their courage, quiet dedication, and willingness to place themselves in harm’s way to protect their community will endure forever.

How will you honor the legacy of these two brave deputies who gave everything to protect their community?

At Tarawa, Saipan, Tinian, and Iwo Jima, it was Smith's amphibious machine that put Marines ashore and kept them supplied. Blunt, demanding, and usually right, he forged the modern Marine Corps in the fire of the island-hopping campaign.

When an active mass shooting broke out near Kraków’s historic Main Square today, sending terrified crowds fleeing through the streets in panic, one heroic Polish police officer ran in the exact opposite direction.

Confronting an assailant armed with a tactical rifle, ballistic helmet, and body armor, the officer engaged the gunman in an open-street shootout. Even after suffering gunshot wounds to his hand and arm, this hero refused to back down, maintained accurate fire through the pain, and neutralized the attacker right on the pavement.

Moments after stopping the attack and shielding countless fleeing civilians from harm, the wounded officer dropped to his knees, calling in emergency medical support and securing the area while nursing his injuries. Polish national leadership commended the officer today for extraordinary heroism, stating that his selfless courage saved dozens of innocent lives.

What goes through an officer’s mind the moment they step into the line of fire to protect people running for their lives?

On May 26, 2008, during a high-stakes daylight direct-action raid against an insurgent compound in Paktya Province, Afghanistan, Army Rangers from the 2nd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment found themselves locked in a point-blank firefight. Leading his junior soldiers through a hostile courtyard, Staff Sgt. Leroy Petry was immediately shot through both legs by enemy AK-47 fire.

Refusing to stay down, Petry dragged himself to cover behind a small courtyard structure alongside two wounded comrades, Specialist Daniel Higgins and Private First Class Lucas Robinson. As insurgent fighters maneuvered to close range, an enemy stick grenade sailed over the wall, landing just feet away from the trapped, wounded Rangers.

With only two seconds before detonation, Petry did not hesitate. Despite bullets tearing through both thighs, he lunged forward toward the explosive, gripped the live grenade in his bare right hand, and hurled it away from his men. The grenade detonated the instant it cleared his grip, severing his right hand and peppering his body with shrapnel.

Petry immediately placed a tourniquet on his own severed wrist, keyed his radio, and calmly continued reporting enemy positions and directing the fight until backup arrived. His instantaneous decision saved both of his fellow Rangers from fatal blast wounds, earning him the Medal of Honor.

What does it say about the mindset of an Army Ranger who willingly trades his own hand to protect the men fighting beside him?

#MedalOfHonor #ArmyRangers #Heroism

Their shark-mouthed P-40s became legends, and Chennault's early-warning net of Chinese spotters let a handful of fighters be everywhere at once. When the U.S. entered the war, he stayed and commanded the Fourteenth Air Force in China to the very end.

When George Kenney arrived in the Southwest Pacific in 1942, MacArthur's air force was a wreck. Within a year, Kenney's Fifth Air Force owned the sky over New Guinea. He invented skip-bombing — bouncing bombs across the water into Japanese ships — and perfected low-level attacks that shredded enemy airfields.

At the Battle of the Bismarck Sea, his pilots destroyed an entire Japanese convoy, proving air power could stop an invasion fleet cold. Brash, brilliant, and utterly devoted to his airmen.

“THE NAVY ADMIRALS WANTED A HEAD ON A PIKE. THEY TRIED TO DESTROY MY 24-YEAR CAREER TO COVER UP THEIR OWN SYSTEMIC FAILURES.”

In February 2022, 24-year-old Navy SEAL candidate Kyle Mullen tragically died of acute bacterial pneumonia just hours after successfully completing the grueling crucible of "Hell Week" in BUD/S Class 352.

While senior Navy leadership scrambled under national media scrutiny, former Basic Training Command commanding officer Captain Brad Geary broke his silence on The Shawn Ryan Show (SRS #124) to expose the institutional blame-shifting and medical oversights behind the tragedy.

In his own words:

“When Kyle Mullen tragically passed away hours after securing Hell Week, it shattered our command.”

“But instead of looking at the systemic medical failures, the rampant use of black-market performance-enhancing drugs among candidates, and the lack of diagnostic monitoring by medical staff, the admirals at the top panicked. They knew the media was circling, and they wanted a quick sacrificial lamb.”

“They launched biased investigations aimed squarely at crucifying me. They leaked my name, stripped my assignments, and tried to bully me into silence so the public wouldn't scrutinize the gross negligence of the medical bureaucracy.”

“I gave 24 years of honorable service to Naval Special Warfare. When you see senior flag officers throw their own commanders under the bus just to save their stars, it shows you how broken military leadership has become.”

Key takeaways from Captain Geary's interview:

Rather than confronting systemic issues within the Navy medical establishment, top flag officers targeted operational leadership to deflect public outrage.

 Extreme physical demands created an environment where candidates concealed life-threatening respiratory symptoms and turned to black-market performance-enhancing drugs to survive training.

Diagnostic protocols failed to adequately monitor candidates during the critical 24-hour post-Hell Week recovery window when acute pulmonary infections frequently manifest.

 True leadership requires senior flag officers to own institutional failures rather than sacrificing 24-year operational commanders to protect their rank.

Walter Krueger led the Sixth Army — 200,000 men — on the long road back across the Pacific: New Guinea, the Admiralties, Morotai, Leyte, Luzon. Island after island, his soldiers clawed back the ground Japan had taken.

He was 63 years old, the oldest field army commander in the Pacific, and he ran his headquarters like a machine. When MacArthur returned to the Philippines, it was Krueger's Sixth Army that made it happen.

Years after putting his life on the line downrange, he found himself trapped in a grueling legal battle—charged with murder alongside fellow operators over high-stakes, split-second decisions made in the fog of war.

The extreme physical and mental crucible of 22 SAS selection

The dark reality of high-threat night raids and close-quarters combat

Rebuilding life, brotherhood, and purpose on the other side of trauma

When the mission is over, who has the warrior's back?

In 1980, after the catastrophic failure of Operation Eagle Claw in the Iranian desert, the U.S. military realized it had a fatal gap: it lacked a dedicated, full-time maritime counter-terrorist assault force.

The Navy turned to a hardened, foul-mouthed Vietnam veteran who had terrorized the Viet Cong so badly in the Mekong Delta that they put a 50,000-piastre bounty on his head: Commander Richard Marcinko.

His mission: build America’s premier maritime counter-terror unit from scratch.

At the time, the Navy only had two active SEAL teams: Team One and Team Two. Marcinko intentionally named his new command SEAL Team Six—a psychological head-fake designed to convince Soviet intelligence that the U.S. had at least four other secret teams operating around the globe.

Marcinko threw out the traditional military rulebook. He hand-selected the deadliest, most aggressive operators in the Navy, gave them unlimited ammunition budgets, and pioneered high-intensity close-quarters battle (CQB) standards that defined modern hostage rescue.

He created the unit that eventually evolved into modern DEVGRU.

Later, the Pentagon tasked him with creating Red Cell—a secret unit made up of rogue SEALs whose job was to infiltrate America’s most secure naval bases and nuclear submarine facilities to expose security flaws using real-world terrorist tactics.

Marcinko broke rules, infuriated pencil-pushing admirals, and fought bureaucracy as ruthlessly as he fought enemies downrange.

He wasn’t a politician. He was a warfighter.

"I lead from the front. I don't send my men into danger; I take them there."

In late 1942, the battle for Buna in New Guinea was going badly. MacArthur sent Robert Eichelberger with blunt orders: take Buna, or don't come back alive. Eichelberger went to the front, fired failing officers, ate the same rations as his men, and took Buna.

He went on to command the Eighth Army through New Guinea and the southern Philippines — one of the finest field commanders of the war, and one of the least remembered. The soldiers who served under him never forgot.

#RobertEichelberger #NewGuinea #Buna #USArmy #WWIIHistory

Across American military installations, active-duty service members are enduring living conditions that would prompt immediate condemnation in any civilian municipality — fighting toxic black mold on their bedroom walls, going without hot water for over a year, and sleeping in personal vehicles during brutal summer heat because their quarters lack functioning air conditioning.
Speaking out on the worsening crisis, Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer detailed the systemic failure following his appointment by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to lead the Pentagon’s Barracks Task Force. Recalling a female service member breaking down in tears over simply wishing for a hot shower, Meyer called the living conditions absolutely heartbreaking and the direct result of decades of institutional neglect.
Independent investigations by the Government Accountability Office have repeatedly documented hazardous barracks across the country, citing raw sewage backups, structural decay, gas leaks, and a staggering 285 billion dollar Department of Defense facilities maintenance backlog. Rather than allowing bureaucratic finger-pointing to stall urgent repairs, Meyer emphasized that the days of passing the buck are finished, stating plainly that if the military fails to fix these quarters, he accepts sole responsibility.
As wall-to-wall inspections begin across 21 major installations nationwide, military leadership faces a critical test — restoring basic human dignity and quality of life to the enlisted troops who volunteer to protect the nation.
#Military #Veterans #Accountability

Four Army Rangers from 3rd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment (3/75) standing on the flightline at sundown before gearing up for a nighttime direct-action raid.

The 75th Ranger Regiment isn't just an elite light infantry unit; they are the premier special operations raid force on the planet.

Throughout two decades of the Global War on Terror, the Rangers maintained an unprecedented operational tempo—conducting high-stakes night raids back-to-back, clearing compounds, eliminating high-value targets, and seizing enemy strongholds in the dead of night.

Behind the night vision goggles, body armor, and suppressed rifles is an uncompromising standard of physical brutality, mental discipline, and sheer violence of action.

They run toward the sound of gunfire when everyone else is running away.

"Recognizing that I volunteered as a Ranger, fully knowing the hazards of my chosen profession, I will always endeavor to uphold the prestige, honor, and high esprit de corps of my Ranger Regiment."

Rangers Lead The Way. All the way.

Marc Mitscher commanded the Fast Carrier Task Force — the most powerful naval striking force ever assembled — through the greatest carrier battles in history: the Philippine Sea, Leyte Gulf, Iwo Jima, Okinawa.

He was a pilot's admiral. At the Philippine Sea, with his planes running out of fuel in the dark, he gave the order no cautious commander would dare: "Turn on the lights." The carriers lit up like cities, guiding exhausted pilots home. Bold when it mattered, beloved always.

America's submarines went to war with torpedoes that didn't work — they ran deep, or didn't explode at all. For eighteen months, sub skippers reported it and were ignored. Then Charles Lockwood took command of the Pacific submarine force and believed his captains.

He ran the tests himself, proved the failures, and fixed the torpedoes. Then he unleashed the wolfpacks. By 1945 his submarines had strangled Japan's merchant fleet and starved an empire. The silent service's greatest victory started with an admiral who listened.

December 8, 2012. The remote mountains of Laghman Province, eastern Afghanistan.

A team from SEAL Team Six (DEVGRU) completed a brutal 4-hour night march up steep mountain terrain on a single mission: rescue American doctor Dilip Joseph, who had been kidnapped by the Taliban.

As the assault force breached the compound, the point man, Chief Petty Officer Nicolas Checque, pushed through six layers of heavy blankets covering the doorway.

Checque was immediately struck by enemy gunfire and mortally wounded.

Senior Chief Edward Byers was the second man in the stack. With bullets tearing through the entryway in pitch darkness, he didn’t flinch.

Byers sprinted directly into the darkened room, engaged an armed guard with an AK-47, and tackled an insurgent to the ground. While physically pinning the enemy fighter to the wall by his throat, he heard an English-speaking voice call out in the dark: "I'm right here!"

Recognizing the hostage, Byers made an instant decision.

He lunged across the room and threw his entire body on top of the hostage, using his chest, Kevlar, and helmet to absorb any incoming gunfire. While shielding Dr. Joseph with his own body, Byers simultaneously pinned another armed insurgent to the ground with his bare hands until the room was cleared.

Dr. Joseph walked out alive.

Chief Nicolas Checque made the ultimate sacrifice and was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross. Senior Chief Edward Byers was awarded the Medal of Honor.

In the darkest room, under direct enemy fire, real operators don't think about self-preservation. They complete the mission.

Drop a 🇺🇸 below to honor Senior Chief Edward Byers Jr. and the fallen Chief Nicolas Checque. Non Sibi Sed Patriae.

Iranian authorities have acknowledged damage to radar infrastructure while continuing to protest foreign military activity in the Gulf waterways.

As international markets and defense analysts closely monitor the Persian Gulf for potential retaliatory moves, Washington has signaled that deterrence remains active while leaving open diplomatic avenues for de-escalation.

The battle of Midway was won before a single B*mb fell — in a basement in Hawaii, by Joseph Rochefort and his codebreakers. His team at Station HYPO cracked enough of the Japanese fleet code to prove Midway was the target, letting Nimitz set the perfect ambush.

Rochefort never got the credit in his lifetime. Office politics pushed him aside, and his work stayed classified for decades. The Navy finally awarded him the Distinguished Service Medal in 1986 — ten years after his death. The codebreaker who saved the Pacific got his salute at last.

Be honest  should every data center in America be legally required to publicly disclose exactly how much water and electricity it consumes each year?

Across the country, the rapid explosion of artificial intelligence and hyperscale cloud infrastructure is driving an unprecedented surge in resource consumption. From Virginia and Texas to Arizona and Georgia, massive server campuses operate around the clock, drawing millions of gallons of water daily for evaporative cooling towers while placing immense strain on regional electrical grids.

Yet despite their massive footprint, many tech conglomerates keep their facility-level utility data tightly guarded under non-disclosure agreements with municipal utility providers. Local residents, agricultural communities, and small business owners frequently face higher utility rates or water conservation warnings while remaining entirely in the dark about how much local capacity is diverted to power AI clusters.

Advocates argue that transparency is a matter of basic public accountability. When public aquifers, regional watersheds, and taxpayer-backed power grids are at stake, citizens deserve to know the real cost of keeping the digital economy running.

Conversely, tech developers contend that detailed consumption figures constitute proprietary operational data that could expose server capacity and competitive trade secrets to rival firms.

Don’t Americans deserve to know the true footprint of the data centers operating in their backyards?

What do you think?

A 26-year-old Venezuelan national who entered the United States illegally is in federal custody after being apprehended by the U.S. Secret Service near the White House with a cache of weapons, telling investigators that voices in his head instructed him to travel to Washington to kill President Donald Trump.

According to federal affidavits and statements released by the Department of Homeland Security, officers approached Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chirinos around 11:42 p.m. Thursday as he was asleep inside a parked Ford F-150 on Constitution Avenue. The vehicle had previously been reported stolen. What began as a routine welfare check rapidly escalated when Guanipa Chirinos used Google Translate on his mobile phone to inform officers that he had firearms in the truck that he wanted to turn over to authorities.

Upon searching the vehicle, Secret Service personnel recovered a disassembled AR-15 style rifle, a MAC-10 handgun, a Glock 43X pistol, extended magazines, and dozens of rounds of loose and boxed ammunition. During subsequent questioning, the suspect stated that he had been living in the stolen truck, purchased the weapons roughly a month prior, and drove to the nation’s capital following internal auditory hallucinations commanding him to assassinate the president.

Records confirm Guanipa Chirinos crossed the southern border unlawfully near Eagle Pass, Texas, in March 2024, where he was processed by Border Patrol and released into the interior. Following his arrest, Immigration and Customs Enforcement lodged an immigration detainer with the U.S. Marshals Service, where he remains held on multiple federal weapons charges.

He made mistakes, and he knew it. But no one ever doubted his heart. When Japan surrendered, Halsey was there on the Missouri's deck, watching the war he had sworn to win come to its end.

Two years later he did it again at the Philippine Sea, destroying Japan's carrier air power for good. He never sought glory, never wrote memoirs, never bragged. His fellow admirals just called him the finest naval commander of the war.

The Lakewood Police Department has officially identified the officer killed in the line of duty during Thursday night’s shooting as Agent Nic Graham.

Agent Graham, badge number 2150, joined the department in 2019 after graduating from the academy. Over five years of dedicated service to the city of Lakewood, he earned widespread respect among his peers, including being honored with the department’s Special Investigations Unit Wingman Award in 2023 for exemplary teamwork and tactical support.

The tragic confrontation unfolded around 6:30 PM on Thursday, November 5, when Lakewood agents tracked an armed suspect boarding an RTD transit bus near Colfax Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard. As officers moved in to make contact, the suspect immediately opened fire.

Agents returned fire and neutralized the gunman on scene. During the intense close-quarters shootout, four Lakewood police agents and one civilian bystander were struck by gunfire. Agent Graham was rushed to the hospital with catastrophic injuries where he tragically succumbed to his wounds.

Law enforcement agencies, first responders, and community members across Colorado have joined in mourning the loss of a courageous public servant who made the ultimate sacrifice while running toward danger to protect innocent transit riders.

Newly released security footage has revealed the terrifying split-second gunfight where an armed U.S. Marine Corps veteran confronted and neutralized an active shooter inside a massive corporate office campus in Tampa, Florida.

The suspect, identified by law enforcement as 35-year-old Jacob Pearson of Orlando, drove onto the Citibank Center campus armed with a rifle, a handgun, and roughly 90 rounds of ammunition. Investigators revealed Pearson was enraged over an impending court summons regarding an unpaid 2,500 dollar credit card debt.

After ramming his vehicle through a security fence into a courtyard where employees were eating lunch, Pearson shot and killed beloved nine-year Citibank human resources specialist LeAnne Selman.

With his rifle raised and additional ammunition ready, Pearson then advanced directly toward the cafeteria building, sending thousands of terrified employees running for exits or barricading inside offices, breakrooms, and supply closets across the campus.

Stationed inside the facility was John Fraley, a Citibank security officer, vice president of operations, and combat-trained Marine Corps veteran. Rather than retreating, Fraley immediately moved toward the gunfire.

Taking up a tactical position around a hallway corner near the cafeteria entrance, Fraley drew his service handgun and waited for the intruder to breach the doorway. The harrowing surveillance video captured the exact moment Pearson stepped into the hallway with his rifle in hand. In a fraction of a second, Fraley leaned around the wall, engaged the suspect through heavy muzzle flash, and struck Pearson five times during a rapid exchange of gunfire.

Pearson collapsed and was later pronounced dead after being transported to Tampa General Hospital.

Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister praised Fraley as an absolute hero who ran directly toward lethal danger and relied on years of military conditioning to save the lives of over 3,200 employees on site.

When faced with an armed active shooter, how critical is prior military training in overriding fear to make split-second life-or-death decisions?

On December 31, 1941, with Pearl Harbor still smoking, Chester Nimitz took command of a broken Pacific Fleet — most of its battleships on the harbor floor. The quiet Texan didn't panic. He listened to his codebreakers, trusted his carrier admirals, and gambled everything on one battle: Midway.

He won. From that June morning in 1942, the tide never turned back. Nimitz ran the largest ocean war in history from a headquarters in Hawaii, island-hopping across the Pacific for three more years until he stood on the deck of the USS Missouri and signed the surrender that ended it.

General Lemuel Shepherd was the 20th Commandant of the Marine Corps — and the man who led the Corps through the entire Korean War. It was Shepherd who fought to keep Marine aviation under Marine control, who built the Corps back up for Korea, and who watched his Marines hold at Pusan, land at Inchon, and break out of Chosin.

A Marine since 1917, Shepherd had seen the Corps grow from a few thousand men into a force that could turn a war. Korea was his final test, and the Corps passed it.

Twentieth Commandant. First in the hearts of the Marines he led.

The 23rd and 24th of June 2006 would be a crucible of leadership and heroism for an already battle-tested and decorated captain in the U.S. Army’s Special Forces. Captain Sheffield F. Ford III was in charge of some 16 Americans and 46 Afghan Army soldiers during "Operation Kaika" in the Panjawi District of Afghanistan’s Kandahar province.

In the bleak farmland, criss-crossed by ditches and barren expanses, Ford led his unit to "re-establish order" in the contested region, entering a Spartan Afghan village on the 23rd. The dilapidated buildings and mud huts were hiding a Taliban force of unknown strength with one thought on their minds: killing Americans and the Afghan soldiers working to take back their country. In their hastily prepared patrol base, Ford organized a perimeter as night enveloped the isolated Special Forces team and their Afghan allies.

As darkness fell, "all hell [broke] loose." From three directions, rifle, machine gun, and rocket-propelled grenade fire landed and exploded on their position. One of Ford’s squad mates later said they had "not seen this disciplined execution of infantry tactics" by the Taliban. Ford dug his men in to repel the assault.

Moving from position to position, he alternated between barking orders, firing at the enemy, and rallying the Afghan soldiers with him. As the night crept on, the remaining Taliban fighters withdrew and Ford took stock of the situation.

Early the next day, he ordered some of his Special Forces operators to lead a team of Afghans into the suspected Taliban hideout. As the unit engaged the hostiles, it was divided in two when some 200 Taliban fighters poured out, separating the American attackers and surrounding the make-shift patrol base.

Over the radio, Ford was connected with one of the translators who had been leading the mission on the Taliban position. The translator saw two Americans were fighting despite being severely wounded and feared capture at any minute. Knowing the ramifications of being taken alive by the Taliban, the translator told Ford he would, if ordered, end the suffering of the troops and his own life rather than be captured. Ford responded, "We’ve got people coming." Ford organized and launched an effective rescue to recover the translator and wounded troops, even if they were mortally wounded. He would not allow American or Afghan alike to be taken in any condition by the Taliban.

The adversaries fought so close to one another that the terrorists screamed to the Afghan soldiers that, "we can forgive you; just put your weapons down and walk away. We want the Americans alive." The months of training and the ties formed between the Americans and the Afghans were put to the test. Seeing the example of Ford running to each of the beleaguered fighters in the face of constant fire, and remembering all they had endured alongside their American trainers, the Afghan soldiers responded to the Taliban’s offer with well-aimed shots and an unbreakable defense.

Exemplifying the U.S. Special Forces motto, De Opresso Liber (to liberate the oppressed), Ford inspired his Afghan troops to stand up to the Taliban fighters and bring them down. He led an evacuation of all the men under his command, wounded included, out of the village under the cover of Apache attack choppers to ensure all would be safe, while sealing the fate of the insurgents. Ford successfully extricated his men, and the unit had more than 120 confirmed kills. Just as the Americans and Afghans had trained together, they sacrificed together; two American and three Afghan soldiers would not leave the battlefield alive. For his accomplishments in the face of such an overpowering force, Ford was awarded the Silver Star, the nation’s third highest military award.

SHOULD FIREARM SAFETY BE TAUGHT IN EVERY PUBLIC CLASSROOM? Tennessee has become the first state in the nation to mandate annual firearm safety classes for all public and charter school students from kindergarten through 12th grade. The landmark law aims to eliminate accidental childhood shootings by removing the dangerous curiosity around guns and teaching kids exactly what to do if they find an unsecured weapon.

“It will save kids, to be honest with you. It avoids some really bad situations. If we teach children from an early age never to touch a firearm and immediately alert an adult, we take away the curiosity that leads to tragedy.”

 Officer Chad Gann, Wildlife Officer & Firearm Instructor, Tennessee Department of Safety & Homeland Security

How the New Law Works
Statewide Annual Mandate: Under Tennessee Code Ann. § 49-6-1016, all public school districts and charter academies across Tennessee must deliver yearly age-appropriate firearm safety lessons developed in partnership with the Department of Education and the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency (TWRA).

Elementary Curriculum (Grades K–5): Younger children focus strictly on accident avoidance and identifying real firearms versus toys. Lessons reinforce the foundational four-step rule: Stop, don't touch, leave the area, and immediately tell a trusted adult.

Middle & High School Curriculum (Grades 6–12): Older students study safe storage practices, the mechanical risks of handling firearms, hunter safety fundamentals, suicide prevention awareness, and the legal consequences of unlawful possession.

The state statute strictly prohibits live ammunition or working firearms during instruction. Certified School Resource Officers (SROs) and instructors use inert plastic training props, multimedia presentations, and classroom demonstrations.

Supporters emphasize that with over 400 million firearms in circulation across the United States, basic firearm safety is a vital life skill comparable to teaching kids how to swim, look both ways before crossing the street, or practice fire drills. Demystifying guns reduces accidental discharges caused by childish curiosity.

Critics and gun reform advocates contend that the burden of gun safety belongs exclusively on adult gun owners through strict safe-storage laws, arguing that mandatory school instruction risks normalizing weapons in learning environments.

Around 0200 the next morning, Amerine received reconnaissance reports that Taliban vehicles were approaching Tarin Kot from the south. Based upon word from Karzai that any northbound convoy would be Taliban, he gave his response: "Well, smoke 'em."

With the approach of first light, Amerine led his men and a few dozen of Karzai's freedom fighters south from Tain Kot. They planned to take up positions on a mountain from which they could cover the likely Taliban avenue of advance. Enroute, they reached the edge of a plateau that opened into a wide valley. Amerine recounts
It was just perfect terrain to defend from, from there, we had great visibility. We could bomb them as they came through the mountain pass.

In company with the Afghan fighters, ODA 574 established itself on the edge of the plateau. The Special Forces Soldiers set up their laser designators and radios, the combat controllers established communication with the forward air controller loitering overhead. In turn, the air controller began coordinating air support for the coming battle. When, after a few hours, the Taliban convoy entered the valley below Amerine's force, it looked like a scene from "Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome." It included vehicles ranging from Toyota pickups to large trucks outfitted with artillery and anti-aircraft guns. With the Taliban force in the open, Amerine's team began designating targets for air strikes. The effect was immediate and devastating - the lead Taliban vehicles were incinerated.

While ODA 574 continued vectoring aircraft against Taliban targets, Amerine and his men heard shouting and the noise of vehicle engines behind them. The ferocity of the American air strikes had unnerved the accompanying group of Afghan freedom fighters. Confronted with the chaos of battle and a substantial language barrier, Amerine was unable to persuade the fighters to stay on the scene. Knowing that their departure would strand his team without transportation, CPT Amerine and his men jumped into the trucks with the Afghan fighters. They headed back to Tarin Kot where Amerine found Karzai in front of his headquarters, organizing his force. CPT Amerine briefed him on the situation and requested use of the trucks so that his team could go back to the plateau and finish what they'd started.

"IF THE TALIBAN GOT PAST US, WE LOST THE TOWN"

Because the Taliban convoy, by this time, had advanced through the pass and overrun the team's previous position, CPT Amerine led his men south to new positions just outside Tarin Kot. Amerine recalls this was the last line of defense for the town
If the Taliban got past us, we lost the town, I had no real hopes whatsoever of keeping Tarin Kot if the Taliban made it into the town in large numbers. All the aircraft in the world weren't going to help us once the Taliban got into the town and it turned into an urban fight.

As Amerine's team resumed vectoring in aircraft, armed townspeople began to arrive, cheering the destruction of the Taliban convoy. After several hours of close combat, the Special Forces had held their ground. They had engaged the Taliban with their light weapons as well as countless air strikes, decimating the enemy force so that not even the few remaining trucks attempting to flee back to Kandahar escaped.

Over the next few weeks, ODA 574 interdicted Taliban convoys attempting to move north from Kandahar, destroying dozens of Taliban vehicles loaded with the means of war. These actions near Tarin Kot earned Amerine and his team the trust and respect of Hamid Karzai and tribal leaders throughout the area. The success of the combined Afghan and Special Forces team also opened the door for Karzai and Amerine to move on the Taliban stronghold of Kandahar.

"IN THE FACE OF OVERWHELMING ODDS"

By late November 2001, Karzai had assembled a formidable force. He had negotiated several Taliban surrenders and begun the work of creating a new governmental structure. With the assistance of ODA 574 he was ready to move south against the Taliban in Kandahar. Leading this effort, CPT Amerine organized the advance in two elements of freedom fighters. He gathered a contingent of 150 Afghans and half of his Special Forces team into one element under his control. The remainder of his team with another force of Afghans were to follow a few hours behind.

On December 3rd, after a pitched street-by-street battle, the freedom fighters seized the town of Showali Kot. Directing in AC-130 gunship support, they also fended off a Taliban counterattack that threatened to surround the town.

Thereafter, CPT Amerine's objective was to seize the lone bridge that crossed the Arghandab, a major river between Tarin Kot and Kandahar. While traversing the last major ridgeline before the Arghandab River, his force came under fire from Taliban in the town of Sayyd Alma Kalaya below the ridge. After a fierce firefight, Amerine's force drove the Taliban off and took the town.

Throughout the night and into the next morning, Amerine's team fought off Taliban counterattacks, engaging the enemy in close combat and with air strikes. The following afternoon, as the enemy fire died down, the first element of an American command team arrived by helicopter.

With the arrival of leaders from his battalion headquarters, Captain Amerine and his team recovered to a hill near Sayyd Alma Kalaya and, for the first time in a long time, got a good night's sleep. On December 5th, the Taliban sent a delegation to surrender Kandahar.

For his contributions in leading ODA 574, Captain Amerine was awarded the Bronze Star with "V" Device. In part, his award citation states that his actions in the face of overwhelming odds and direct hostile aggression resulted in the surrender of Kandahar by the Taliban forces .. directly contributed to his unit's and his country's success

"THE GREATEST PRIVILEGE OF MY LIFE"

After returning from Afghanistan, the Army selected Captain Amerine to join the faculty at the United States Military Academy at West Point. As with his preparation to become a Green Beret, this new undertaking entailed a substantial period of education and development. The Army assigned Captain Amerine as a student at theGeorge Bush School of Government at Texas A&M University. For 18 months, Jason focused his attention on graduate studies in international relations. Thereafter, he joined the faculty at West Point, where as an Assistant Professor of International Relations, he assumed the mantel of mentoring and developing a new generation of Soldiers. Just as other Soldiers had prepared him to dominate the challenges of life and battle, he now set about preparing West Point cadets for challenges they would face in the defense of freedom. Today he states
Serving as an officer in the United States Army has been the greatest privilege of my life. In Afghanistan, I commanded American and Afghan soldiers, each fighting for his own nation and his people, yet united in a common cause as they entrusted one another with their lives. There is no greater courage than for people to fight side-by-side against the terrible odds they faced with such impenetrable faith in one another.

THE PRESIDENT: Please be seated. Good afternoon. And on behalf of Michelle and myself, welcome to the White House. And thank you, General Carver, for that beautiful invocation.

We are a nation of more than 300 million Americans. Of these, less than 1 percent wears the uniform of our Armed Services. And of these, just a small fraction has earned the badges of our Special Operations Forces. 

In the finest military the world has ever known, these warriors are the best of the best. In an era that prizes celebrity and status, they are “quiet professionals” — never seeking the spotlight. In a time of war, they have borne a burden far beyond their small numbers — training foreign militaries to stand on their own; bringing schools and medicine to remote villages; and taking to the terrorists and insurgents who plot against us.

Few Americans ever see their service, but all Americans are safer because of it. And our hearts swell with pride just hearing their names, including the legendary Green Berets. Today, it is my privilege to present our nation's highest military decoration — the Medal of Honor — to one of these remarkable soldiers, Staff Sergeant Robert J. Miller.

To do so, we are joined by Vice President Biden, and from the Miller's family's home state of Florida, a leader who helped make this day possible, Congresswoman Suzanne Kosmas.

We are joined by leaders from across my administration, including Secretary of Defense Robert Gates; Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Admiral Mike Mullen; and leaders from our Armed Forces, including Army Secretary John McHugh and Chief of Staff General George Casey, as well as Commander of Special Operations Command, Admiral Eric Olson.
 
We are honored to be joined by Rob's fellow soldiers in whose ranks he served — his teammates from Alpha Company, 3rd Battalion, 3rd Special Forces Group from Fort Bragg, and those who now welcome him into their ranks, members of the Medal of Honor Society.

Most of all, we welcome more than 100 of Rob's friends and family, especially his father Phil, his mother Maureen and his many brothers and sisters.

It has been said that courage is not simply one of the virtues, but the form of every virtue at the testing point. For Rob Miller, the testing point came nearly three years ago, deep in a snowy Afghan valley. But the courage he displayed that day reflects every virtue that defined his life.

Rob was wise beyond his years. Growing up in Wheaton, Illinois, outside of Chicago, he was the boy in school who penned a poem about American GI's in World War II, men — like the soldier Rob would become himself — who he said fought day and night, fighting for what they thought was right.

Rob was born to lead — the high school gymnast who trained so hard his coach had to kick him out at night so they could close the gym. He was the Army recruit who pushed himself to his limits — both physically and mentally — to earn the title Green Beret. He was the Special Forces soldier who, on his first tour in Afghanistan, earned two Army Commendation Medals for his valor.

Devotion to duty. An abiding sense of honor. A profound love of country. These were the virtues that found their ultimate expression when Rob — just 24 years old and on his second tour — met his testing point on January 25, 2008.

Rob and his team were in the remote northwest of Afghanistan. Their mission: clear a valley of insurgents who had been attacking Afghan forces and terrorizing villagers. So when they came across an insurgent compound, Rob and his men made their move, unleashing their fire and calling in airstrikes.

Now, they were on foot, heading over to that destroyed compound, to assess the damage and gather intelligence. It was still dark, just before dawn. It was freezing cold — and silent, except for the crackle of their radios and the crunch of snow under their boots. Like so many times before, Rob was up front — leading a patrol of two dozen Afghans and Americans on a narrow trail along the valley floor, the steep mountains towering over them.

First, it was just a single insurgent, jumping out from behind a boulder. Then, the whole valley seemed to explode with gunfire. Within seconds, Rob and his patrol were pinned down, with almost no cover — bullets and rocket-propelled grenades raining down from every direction. And when enemy reinforcements poured in, the odds were overwhelming. Rob's small patrol of two dozen men was nearly surrounded by almost 150 insurgents.

With the enemy just feets away — some so close he could see their faces — Rob held his ground. Despite the chaos around him, he radioed back enemy positions. As the only Pashto speaker on his team, he organized the Afghan soldiers around him. But the incoming fire, in the words of one soldier, was simply “astounding.”

Rob made a decision. He called for his team to fall back. And then he did something extraordinary. Rob moved in the other direction — toward the enemy, drawing their guns away from his team and bringing the fire of all those insurgents down upon himself.

The fighting was ferocious. Rob seemed to disappear into clouds of dust and debris, but his team could hear him on the radio, still calling out the enemy's position. And they could hear his weapon still firing as he provided cover for his men. And then, over the radio, they heard his voice. He had been hit. But still, he kept calling out enemy positions. Still, he kept firing. Still, he kept throwing his grenades. And then they heard it — Rob's weapon fell silent.

This is the story of what one American soldier did for his team, but it's also a story of what they did for him. Two of his teammates braved the bullets and rushed to Rob's aid. In those final moments, they were there at his side — American soldiers there for each other.

The relentless fire forced them back, but they refused to leave their fallen comrade. When reinforcements arrived, these Americans went in again — risking their lives, taking more casualties — determined to bring Rob Miller out of that valley. And finally, after fighting that raged for hours, they did.

When the dust settled and the smoke cleared, there was no doubt Rob Miller and his team had struck a major blow against the local insurgency. Five members of his patrol had been wounded, but his team had survived. And one of his teammates surely spoke for all of them when he said of Rob, “I would not be alive today if not for his ultimate sacrifice.”

This is the valor that America honors today. To Rob's family and friends, I know that no words can ease the ache in your hearts. But I also know this — Rob's life and legacy endures.

Rob endures in the pride of his parents. Phil and Maureen, you raised a remarkable son. Today and in the years to come, may you find some comfort in knowing that Rob gave his life doing what he loved — protecting his friends and defending his country. You gave your oldest son to America, and America is forever in your debt.

Rob endures in the love of his brothers and sisters, all seven of whom join us today. Your brothers laid down his life so you could live yours in security and freedom. You honor him by living your lives to the fullest, and I suspect Rob would be especially proud of his younger brother Tom, who, inspired by his big brother, is now training to be a Green Beret himself.

Rob endures in the Afghans that he trained and he befriended. In valleys and villages half a world away, they remember him — the American who spoke their language, who respected their culture and who helped them defend their country. They welcomed him into their homes and invited him to their weddings. And in a sign of their lasting gratitude, they presented Rob's parents with a beautiful Afghan flag — Afghan rug, which hangs today in the Miller home, a symbol of the partnership between the people of America and Afghanistan.

Rob Miller endures in the service of his teammates — his brothers in arms who served with him, bled with him and fought to bring him home. These soldiers embody the spirit that guides our troops in Afghanistan every day — the courage, the resolve, the relentless focus on their mission: to break the momentum of the Taliban insurgency, and to build the capacity of Afghans to defend themselves, and to make sure that Afghanistan is never again a safe haven for terrorists who would attack our country. That is their mission, that is our mission, and that is what we will do. And I would ask Rob's team, who were with him that day, to please stand and be recognized. (Applause.)

Finally, Rob Miller — and all those who give their lives in our name — endure in each of us. Every American is safer because of their service. And every American has a duty to remember and honor their sacrifice.

If we do — if we keep their legacy alive, if we keep faith with the freedoms they died to defend — then we can imagine a day, decades from now, when another child sits down at his desk, ponders the true meaning of heroism and finds inspiration in the story of a soldier — Staff Sergeant Robert J. Miller and a generation that “fought day and night, fighting for what they thought was right.”

That is the meaning of this medal. And that is our summons today, as a proud and grateful nation. So please join me in welcoming Phil and Maureen Miller for the reading of the citation. (Applause.)

(AFNS - 9/26/2011) -- As the only qualified joint terminal attack controller in an operation Oct. 5, 2009, an Air Force Special Operations Command combat controller knew the ground situation would be dire if he died. As an armor-piercing round entered his left shoulder and wreaked havoc throughout his chest, he said his focus wasn't on his young family in North Carolina. It was on his team.

"I've seen those types of injuries before, and time isn't your friend," said the Air Force Cross recipient Staff Sgt. Robert Gutierrez Jr "I thought -- I have three minutes before I'm going to die. I've got to do something big. Based on that time frame, I'm going to change the world in three minutes."

The team of 30 U.S. Army Special Forces and Afghan National Army commandos was surrounded in a "Taliban-sympathetic village" in the Herat province of Afghanistan. According to officials' reports, enemy fighters were positioned on rooftops just 10-feet from the team's position inside a neighboring building. Gutierrez was shot during the 4-hour firefight that included sniper and small-arms fire as well as rocket propelled grenades.

As the combat controller, Gutierrez was the only qualified radio operator communicating with Airmen overhead to provide close-air support and real-time battlefield surveillance, which was critical for the team's mission and for evacuating their wounded.
"Combat controllers are the air-to-ground interface, bringing the firepower and communications links to the ground force commander," Gutierrez said. "We bring an extraordinary amount of firepower in a small package (that is) able to shoot, move and communicate at the same time."

Believing he was about to die, the San Diego native refused to remove his body armor, which held his radio, despite two medics repeatedly ordering him to take it off so his wounds could be treated. Gutierrez only relented momentarily, allowing the medic to insert a needle decompression tube just below his collarbone.

A sucking chest wound, which is common in gunshot victims, fills the chest cavity with blood, collapsing the lungs. The medic's procedure released the growing pressure on his collapsed lung, allowing Gutierrez to breathe and speak -- so he got back on the radio. He continued to advise the ground force commander and request close air support of F-16 Fighting Falcons and A-10 Thunderbolt IIs overhead.
